vignette:
The bus station is crowded, morning rush, the air thick with sweat and diesel. He is a young librarian, thirty-two, waiting to go to work. He carries a briefcase with overdue notices and a new acquisition-a biography of Kwame Nkrumah. Then the world folds in on itself. A sound that is not a sound, just a pressure that lifts him off his feet and throws him against a concrete pillar. Dust. Screaming. A shoe lying alone. His left ear rings with a high, steady pitch that will never fully stop.

He crawls. He does not know for how long. He finds a child's sandal and holds it until a rescue worker pries it from his hand. They take him to a hospital-he has a broken clavicle, a concussion, and a deep gash on his forearm from flying glass. But the real injury is something else, something that settles into his bones like a cold groundwater. He does not speak for three days. When he does, it is only to ask about his wife. She was not at the station. She is fine. He is not.

That was forty-six years ago. He is now seventy-eight, a retired head librarian who still works part-time at a small public branch in a quiet suburb. He catalogues donated books every Tuesday and Thursday. His hands are steady, but his eyes never stop moving. He checks the exits of every room he enters-the reading room, the staff break room, the restroom-as if by habit. But it is not habit. It is a calculus he cannot disable. Three exits, two windows, distance to the nearest cover. He knows the layout of this library better than anyone, but he maps it only for escape.

He avoids the section on modern world history. He has not reshelved a book on the Middle East or terrorism in twenty years. His supervisor assumes it is a matter of preference. It is not. The sight of the word "bomb" on a spine makes his stomach drop. He once-three years ago-opened a donated book and found a photograph of a bus station tucked between pages. He dropped the book, left the building, and walked for two hours without knowing where he was going. His wife found him sitting on a bench near the courthouse, staring at his hands.

The noise at the library is low, but certain sounds still trigger him. A balloon popping during a children's program sends him flat against the wall. A patron dropping a stack of books makes him flinch so hard that he drops his own. He has learned to brace himself before the automatic door hisses open. He always stands with his back to a shelf, never to an open aisle. His colleagues call him careful, maybe a little eccentric. They do not know that he sleeps with a baseball bat next to the bed. They do not know that he cannot go to the grocery store on weekends because the crowds feel like a bus station.

His wife of fifty-two years knows. She understands when he wakes at 3:00 a.m. drenched in sweat, still hearing that pressure in his chest. She has learned not to touch him from behind. She says, "You're here. You're safe." But the word "safe" does not stick. It slides off him like water off oil.

He continues to work because the routine holds him together. He alphabetizes, cross-indexes, mends torn spines. There is order in the Dewey Decimal System-a world where everything has its place and nothing explodes. But even here, he cannot stop scanning the shadows, listening for the low rumble that might be a bus or might be the end of everything. The library is quiet. His hands are still. But inside, the bus station is always morning rush, and the bomb is always about to go off.
